title: Week 10 Mastery Quiz — Byzantium and the Islamic World

questions.prompt: Which statement most accurately describes the polity historians commonly call the Byzantine Empire?
choices: It was a new state unrelated to Rome.
Its inhabitants consistently called themselves Byzantines rather than Romans.
It was the eastern Roman Empire, whose institutions and identity changed across centuries.
It abandoned Roman law when Constantinople became its capital.
questions.explanation: The Byzantine Empire was the continuation of the eastern Roman Empire; Byzantine is a later historical label.

questions.prompt: Why is the phrase ‘the Islamic Empire’ often too imprecise for the period studied this week?
choices: Islam had no relationship to political history.
All Muslim-ruled territories were independent city-states.
Arabic was never used in government.
Different caliphates, dynasties, regions, and communities changed across time and were not one uniform political system.
questions.explanation: The Islamic world contained changing and diverse political formations rather than one timeless state.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes sharia historically?
choices: A broad Islamic moral and legal tradition developed through interpretation of religious sources in varied historical contexts
A single modern-style statute book applied identically everywhere
A Byzantine legal code translated into Arabic
A tax imposed only on merchants
questions.explanation: Sharia is a broad interpretive moral-legal tradition, not one uniform historical statute book.

questions.prompt: What can Justinian’s legal compilation best help historians investigate?
choices: Only private religious belief
Roman legal inheritance and efforts to organize imperial law in the sixth-century eastern Roman Empire
The complete daily experience of every Byzantine subject
Abbasid scientific practice
questions.explanation: The compilation is evidence for legal inheritance and imperial organization, but cannot alone establish universal lived experience.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation of translation movements is strongest?
choices: Translation merely copied texts word for word and produced no intellectual change.
Translation always improved every source.
Translation could preserve selected works while commentary, terminology, criticism, synthesis, and testing also transformed knowledge.
Translation occurred only from Greek directly into Latin.
questions.explanation: Translation networks involved preservation and intellectual transformation.

questions.prompt: Which evidence would best test a claim that a legal principle affected everyday life?
choices: The legal text alone
A modern map of the empire
A vocabulary definition
Local court, administrative, documentary, material, or narrative evidence showing implementation or response
questions.explanation: Local and independent evidence is needed to investigate implementation and lived practice.

questions.prompt: Why should a map connecting Baghdad, Constantinople, Cairo, and Córdoba be interpreted cautiously?
choices: A line between cities can suggest a possible connection but cannot by itself prove frequency, direction, volume, or direct personal contact.
Cities cannot be mapped historically.
All knowledge traveled by sea.
The cities existed in exactly the same political system.
questions.explanation: Spatial visualization shows relationships and hypotheses, not automatic proof of movement or causation.

questions.prompt: Which statement best represents multilingual scholarship in the period?
choices: Knowledge moved through only one language at a time and scholars avoided earlier traditions.
Scholars working across languages and institutions could translate, preserve, criticize, synthesize, and extend earlier knowledge.
Only rulers participated in intellectual exchange.
Religious difference prevented scholarly exchange in every setting.
questions.explanation: Multilingual and multi-institutional networks supported varied forms of preservation and innovation.

questions.prompt: Which claim avoids a misleading single-civilization narrative?
choices: One civilization alone preserved all ancient knowledge for the modern world.
Every society contributed equally to every intellectual field.
Knowledge changed through selective preservation, loss, translation, patronage, criticism, exchange, and innovation across multiple communities.
Political institutions had no effect on scholarship.
questions.explanation: Historical knowledge networks were selective, uneven, multi-directional, and shaped by many actors and institutions.

questions.prompt: Which research design would best answer whether translation transformed knowledge?
choices: Count translated titles without reading any evidence.
Assume every difference is a translation error.
Use only a modern encyclopedia summary.
Compare an earlier text, one or more translations/commentaries, and later scholarly use while tracking provenance, terminology, changes, and uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Comparative provenance across texts, translations, commentary, and later use can reveal preservation and transformation.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least three specific pieces of evidence and at least two source types, explain how cities, states, religious/legal institutions, and multilingual scholarly networks preserved, debated, and created knowledge across Byzantine and Islamic-world contexts. Include one limitation or uncertainty in the surviving evidence.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a defensible claim, uses accurate evidence across more than one political or cultural context, explains at least one mechanism of preservation and one of transformation or innovation, tracks evidence provenance, and acknowledges a meaningful limitation.
